r: This foundations course builds entry-level competence in the nurse-patient relationship, therapeutic and multicultural communication, and basic psychomotor skills practiced in a facilitated simulation laboratory and a supervised clinical practicum inside a health care facility. These are hands-on, real-time, in-person tasks: reading a patient's affect, adjusting communication to culture and literacy, and performing supervised procedures under direct preceptor observation. Task-exposure research finds manual, physical, and real-time interpersonal work among the least exposed categories, and observed AI usage concentrates in computer and writing tasks rather than embodied clinical skill-building. AI tools may support documentation templates or pre-briefing for simulation scenarios, but the clinical practicum hours themselves are dictated by the program's Colorado Board of Nursing-approved curriculum, which requires supervised in-person skill demonstration before progression. At this horizon, adoption of any AI substitute for supervised hands-on skill acquisition is negligible.

By the five-year horizon, ambient documentation and AI-generated care-plan drafts will likely be more common in the simulation and practicum settings this course uses, plausibly easing some charting burden for students and preceptors. Core tasks remain resistant, however: performing a supervised procedure, reading nonverbal patient cues, and demonstrating therapeutic communication under evaluation require physical presence and real-time judgment that current systems do not replicate. Productivity research on customer support and writing tasks shows meaningful gains from AI assistance, but those gains cluster in text-heavy, low-stakes work, not psychomotor skill verification by a preceptor. Because clinical practicum hours are a hard, course-specific requirement embedded in the Board-approved curriculum needed for licensure eligibility, the instrumental need to physically complete this course is unlikely to loosen much even as adjacent administrative tasks become more automatable. Confidence in this trajectory is moderate given how quickly clinical documentation tools are diffusing.

Ten years out, capability trends suggest AI systems will handle longer, more complex tasks, and some simulation-lab pre-work or feedback on communication technique could plausibly be AI-augmented by then. Still, this course's foundational purpose is licensure-track psychomotor and interpersonal skill formation delivered through supervised, in-person practicum hours in a health care facility, and Colorado Board of Nursing curriculum approval processes change slowly relative to model capability. Diffusion research indicates AI adoption remains uneven and lags raw capability even in digitally native industries, and hands-on clinical training is a poor candidate for early substitution regardless of frontier progress. This is a genuinely uncertain horizon: better haptic or simulation-integrated AI tools are plausible, but nothing in the current evidence base supports assuming the clinical-practicum requirement itself becomes optional. The course also sits early in the nursing sequence, so its instrumental necessity is reinforced by downstream prerequisite dependencies regardless of AI capability.
NURA 3020.d: In this course, students will be introduced to the profession of nursing and the culture of the health care environment. The core knowledge, core competencies, and role development of the professional nurse are explored. Students begin to develop an understanding of human responses to health and illness within the nurse-patient relationship. Students begin to apply the nursing process, critical thinking, clinical reasoning, and therapeutic and multicultural communication. Practice environments for the development of basic nursing skills include the facilitated simulation laboratory and a clinical practicum in a health care facility.

The course sits inside the nursing major's required curriculum, which the Colorado Board of Nursing must approve as a whole, giving it a programmatic mandate even though it carries no clinical clock hours of its own. At this horizon, AI functions at most as a drafting aid for case write-ups, not a substitute for the course's judgment work.

Within five years, AI drafting assistance for ethics case papers and discussion-board responses will likely be widespread among students, and some of the course's lower-order content delivery -- summarizing ethical frameworks, generating discussion prompts -- could shift toward AI-assisted formats. The core instrumental task, however, remains applying professional judgment to a specific dilemma where errors carry real consequences for patients and licensure, a verification burden that keeps a human ethicist or instructor in the loop. Jagged-frontier findings show AI users outside a model's competence zone perform noticeably worse with misplaced confidence, and contextual ethical reasoning in patient care is a plausible candidate for that failure mode given its ambiguity and stakes. Because the course still contributes to the Board-approved nursing curriculum without itself gating licensure through clock hours, its institutional protection is moderate rather than absolute. Confidence here is medium: the direction is stable, but the pace of change in how ethics is taught is harder to forecast.

The binding constraint is less about clinical embodiment here and more about verification burden: professional ethical judgment in ambiguous, high-stakes patient scenarios resists confident automation because failure modes are non-obvious and consequences fall on real patients and the nurse's license. NURA 3160.d: The course prepares the professional nursing student to analyze ethical issues that emerge in the practice of nursing. The Magnet/Pathway's to Excellence concept of Exemplary Practice and the QSEN competencies of Patient-Centered Care, Teamwork and Collaboration, and Evidence-Based Practice are explored as they relate to ethics and professional nursing. Students apply critical thinking concepts to applicable codes of ethics, ethical theories, principles, and rules in discussing the ethical dilemmas encountered in professional practice. Values and beliefs are examined in the context of ethical issues, role development, and application in health care.

Course content aligns with the Magnet/Pathway to Excellence concepts including Empirical Outcomes, Exemplary Professional Practice, New Knowledge, Innovations, and Improvements, and QSEN Competencies of EBP and Patient-Centered Care. NURA 3410.d: Clinical pharmacology covers the major principles of pharmacology, drug classifications, and pharmacotherapy. The nursing process, legal, ethical, cultural, and social values are also discussed in relationship to various disease processes and complex patient situations. Drug calculations are also covered. Critical thinking, communication, and safe medication administration is integrated in the course.

NURA 3500.d: The focus of this course is on the application of foundational mental health nursing concepts and interventions in the care of patients. This course includes the application of developmental theories and ethical principles to the nursing care of mental health patients. Emphasis is placed on therapeutic communication techniques, health promotion and relapse prevention. Students apply the nursing process using critical thinking and decision-making skills while providing safe, basic care to selected patients.

NURA 3700.d: This course is designed for students to develop, practice, and demonstrate their health assessment competence. The student collects and organizes data to obtain a complete health history and perform a physical examination. Students have an opportunity to practice interviewing skills and physical examination techniques. Emphasis is placed on the use of critical thinking and demonstration of a physical examination while caring for individuals. Focus is on utilization of core knowledge and core competencies related to the care of adults with basic and intermediate alterations in health. NURA 4000.d: Students in this course gain the tools for critically analyzing the principles of health promotion and disease prevention of families, groups, and communities. NURA 4040.d: In this course, the student is introduced to the process of collecting and analyzing data used to improve the quality of care patients receive and enhance their safety. The course operates inside a Colorado Board of Nursing-approved curriculum with required clinical hours, meaning the instrumental need for enrollment is currently fully intact and not meaningfully reduced by any deployed AI tool.

Over five years, care-coordination software and documentation assistants may spread further into pediatric settings, consistent with capability trends showing rapid gains in task-time horizons AI can handle. Still, the course's substance, physical pediatric assessment, administering care to children, and health teaching delivered through direct interpersonal rapport with families, remains embodied and psychomotor in nature. Task-exposure research continues to classify manual, real-time caregiving work as low-exposure relative to writing- or programming-heavy occupations. The verification burden stays at its floor: pediatric safety errors are high-cost and often non-obvious, so a supervising nurse's judgment cannot be replaced by model output. Diffusion data shows adoption of AI tools remains uneven across healthcare institutions even where the technology exists. Given the persistent Board of Nursing clinical-hour mandate, the instrumental need for this course's simulation and clinical components should remain close to its current level, with only incremental administrative augmentation likely.

At ten years the honest position is uncertainty bounded by structural constraints. Model capability may extend well beyond current limits, and some pediatric triage-support or family education materials could be AI-generated by then with clinician review. However, the embodied core of this course, hands-on pediatric assessment, comforting a frightened child, reading subtle nonverbal distress signals, and building trust with families under stress, sits squarely in the territory the jagged-frontier findings describe as outside AI's reliable competence, where confident but wrong outputs are hardest to catch. Licensure curricula approved by the Board of Nursing change slowly relative to model progress, and macro estimates of AI's productivity effect over a decade remain modest. Some augmentation of the theoretical and documentation portions is plausible, but the clinical practicum requirement anchoring this course to direct, supervised pediatric care is unlikely to be rendered instrumentally unnecessary within this horizon.

At five years, productivity research on professional writing, showing meaningfully faster drafting with quality gains, suggests the policy-analysis, business-economics, and organizational-theory writing components of this course could see real augmentation, and GitHub Copilot-scale speedups illustrate how fast such assistance can compound in analytical domains. The interpersonal leadership tasks, coordinating teams, negotiating conflict, motivating staff, stay resistant to substitution per task-exposure research's finding that non-routine interpersonal work is comparatively low-exposure. Ten years is genuinely uncertain territory, but the directional case for further softening is stronger here than for this program's clinical courses. Macro productivity estimates over a decade remain modest, tempering how far this shift plausibly goes, but this course's instrumental need is more exposed than the clinical, hands-on courses in this batch.

r: Nursing Senior Experience is a capstone practicum in which students synthesize program concepts under a clinical preceptor, developing individualized learning outcomes tied to hands-on patient care. The clinical component maps directly to Assisting and Caring for Others, Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others, and Making Decisions and Solving Problems, all exercised in real clinical settings with real patients under supervision. This is the most embodied, real-time course in the batch: preceptor-guided decision-making, physical care delivery, and interprofessional coordination cannot be replicated by a model regardless of its text or reasoning capability. Observed-usage data confirms AI adoption remains concentrated in digital, computer-mediated work rather than supervised bedside practicum. As the terminal, board-approved clinical requirement capping the nursing curriculum, this course's instrumental need is currently fully intact; no deployed AI tool substitutes for supervised, individualized clinical precepting before licensure eligibility.

Over five years, the structural argument for this course changes little. Its content is not a fixed body of transferable knowledge but a supervised, individualized clinical placement whose value lies precisely in real-time preceptor feedback on a specific student's developing judgment, an inherently embodied, one-to-one activity. Task-exposure research consistently finds manual, real-time, in-person work stays low-exposure even as capability elsewhere accelerates, and productivity RCT gains concentrate in office and writing tasks, not supervised clinical precepting. Verification burden remains at its floor because errors during unsupervised-adjacent capstone practice carry direct patient-safety consequences requiring an expert preceptor's real-time correction. The Colorado Board of Nursing's approval of the curriculum, including this terminal clinical requirement, is not something institutions can bypass by substituting AI tools. Diffusion data shows adoption lagging capability broadly, reinforcing that this course's instrumental role in certifying clinical readiness should remain essentially unchanged at this horizon.

At ten years, meaningful hedging is warranted given how fast underlying model capability could move, and administrative or documentation aspects of precepted practice may be considerably more AI-assisted by then. But the course's core function, an individualized, supervised clinical placement validating a specific student's readiness to practice under real conditions with a real preceptor, is structurally resistant to substitution regardless of how capable AI becomes at answering clinical questions in the abstract. The jagged-frontier research's finding that AI users misjudge accuracy outside a model's competence zone is especially salient for a capstone meant to catch exactly those judgment gaps before independent practice. Licensure-gated curricula change slowly, and macro estimates put AI's productivity effect over a decade at a modest level. This course's terminal, clinical, individualized character makes it the most durable in the batch against any plausible AI-driven reduction in instrumental necessity.
